title: associated anomalies in congenital lung abnormalities: a 20-year experience
display_name: Associated Anomalies in Congenital Lung Abnormalities: A 20-Year Experience
abstract: introduction: a congenital lung abnormality (cla) is often found in conjunction with other abnormalities but screening guidelines for newborns with cla have not yet been reported. we aimed to assess the incidence of associated anomalies in cla patients born or followed up at our centre and the need for additional screening of newborns with a cla. methods: from a retrospective chart review of all patients born with a cla between january 1999 and january 2019, we identified patients diagnosed with a congenital pulmonary airway malformation, bronchopulmonary sequestration, congenital lobar overinflation, bronchogenic cyst, or lung agenesis. associated anomalies were noted and categorized according to the affected organ system. results: twenty-eight (14%) of 196 cla patients had a major associated anomaly. this was most frequent in conjunction with a lung agenesis (100%) or bronchogenic cyst (29%). congenital heart defects (32%) and gastrointestinal defects (18%) were the most frequently associated anomalies. examination of newborns with a cla should focus on the cardiovascular and gastrointestinal tract, and a chest and abdominal radiograph may be useful to assess signs of major associated anomalies, regardless of the clinical course.
classification_path: Medical and Health Science > Clinical Medicine > Internal Medicine > Gastroenterology

title: meningococcal septicaemia: do not be reassured by normal investigations
display_name: Meningococcal septicaemia: do not be reassured by normal investigations
abstract: this paper reports a case of meningococcal septicaemia. this case shows that normal investigations may provide the unwary clinician with an unfounded reassurance when dealing with children with this serious infection.

title: persistent mullerian duct syndrome with polysplenia and short pancreas: a case report
display_name: Persistent Mullerian Duct Syndrome with Polysplenia and Short Pancreas: A Case Report
abstract: persistent mullerian duct syndrome is a rare entity and usually presents with common symptoms of undescended testis and hernia. the syndrome is caused by an insufficient amount of mullerian inhibiting substance or due to the insensitivity of the target organ to mullerian inhibiting substance. polysplenia is a rare congenital disease manifested by multiple small accessory spleens. the association of these two entities is rare and has not been reported in the literature. we reported a case of a 27 years old male presented with complains of right flank pain and nausea. ultrasound showed right ureteric calculus with hydronephrosis and elongated soft tissue mass posterior to bladder. contrast enhanced computed tomography showed soft tissue suggestive of infantile uterine structure with multiple splenculi and short pancreas. he was diagnosed as persistent mullerian duct syndrome with unilateral cryptorchidism, polysplenia and short pancreas, coincidentally detected while evaluating for ureteric colic.
classification_path: Medical and Health Science > Clinical Medicine > Internal Medicine > Gastroenterology

title: upper gastrointestinal series in children: what surgeons need to know
display_name: Upper gastrointestinal series in children: what surgeons need to know
abstract: abstract background upper gastrointestinal (ugi) series is the standard imaging tool for diagnosis of structural and functional abnormalities affecting the esophagus, stomach, and proximal small bowel. the aim of this study was to delineate the clinical indications for ugi series in children that are associated with the presence of significant radiological abnormalities aiming for more standardized care for those patients. results ugi series of 118 patients was analyzed with calculation of clinical score. vomiting was the most frequent primary complaint (63.6%), followed by dysphagia and recurrent chest infection. forty-nine patients had positive upper gi findings (42%). the most detected abnormality was related to the stomach and duodenum (21.4%). variable degrees of idiopathic gastroesophageal reflux were detected in 16 patients (13.6%). patients with clinical score 2 or more had significantly more prevalence of abnormal findings ( p = .001). vomiting (especially when bilious), underweight, aspiration, and recurrent chest infection were strong predictors of abnormal findings on upper gi series ( p = 0.007, 0.001, 0.009, and 0.001, respectively) and increased the diagnostic yield of upper gi series for detection of abnormalities by 3.48, 9.6, 4, and 4.12 times, respectively. conclusion diagnostic yield of ugi series was relatively higher in patients having two or more symptoms (clinical score 2 or more) and in children with bilious vomiting, aspiration and underweight, or repeated chest infection.

abstract: these results show that small intestinal manometry is useful not only as an aid in diagnosing the aetiology of ciip presenting in infancy, but also in predicting outcome.

title: duodenal atresia and hirschsprung diseasein a patient with down syndrome
display_name: Duodenal Atresia and Hirschsprung Diseasein a Patient with Down Syndrome
abstract: a two days-old newborn female patient with down syndrome was admitted to our hospital with complaint of vomiting. physical examination was unremarkable except for the typical physical appearance of down syndrome. an abdominal radiography showed the double-bubble sign, characteristic for duodenal obstruction, and the patient was operated with prediagnosis of duodenal atresia. however, during the operation, hirschsprung s disease was suspected and the diagnosis was confirmed by rectal biopsy. in this study, we described the case of duodenal atresia together with hirschsprung s disease in a patient with down syndrome. radiologists and pediatric surgeons should consider this issue for a correct diagnosis and treatment.

title: prenatal and postnatal peculiarities and consequences of intestinal loop patency disorder with expansive giant cystic abdominal mass in a preterm newborn
display_name: Prenatal and postnatal peculiarities and consequences of intestinal loop patency disorder with expansive giant cystic abdominal mass in a preterm newborn
abstract: the cyst anatomically communicated with the aboral section of the jejunum, but the lumen of the jejunum was functionally obturated by solid whitish masses. the histological examination confirmed the diagnostic features of a cyst of intestinal origin. the ileum and colon were patent throughout, but of smaller diameter, so a bishop-koop relieving anastomosis was indicated. the condition of the child at the age of 9 months was stabilised and surgical closure of the stoma was carried out (tab. 1, fig. 8, ref. 21). text in pdf www.elis.sk keywords: newborn, jejunal atresia, intestinal cyst.

title: 'critical' ultrasound: the new essential skill in pediatric cardiac intensive care unit (pcicu)
display_name: 'Critical' ultrasound: the new essential skill in Pediatric Cardiac Intensive Care Unit (PCICU)

authorships.name: Mahmoud Elbarbary
institutions: King Saud bin Abdulaziz University for Health Sciences

authorships.name: Mohammad Kabbani
institutions: King Saud bin Abdulaziz University for Health Sciences

abstract: with the recent introduction of a high-quality, reasonably priced, and completely portable pediatric/neonatal ultrasound (us) machines, a new philosophy of us imaging emerged which is the critical ultrasound . this is a paradigm shift from being organ-based, systematic, comprehensive diagnostic exam done by radiologists to a new concept of problem-based , goal-directed, focused multi-organ, time-dependent, exam done by the treating intensivist. based on this concept, the us exam is not done for an organ (e.g. us for abdomen or chest) but rather done to enhance the management of a problem (us for hypotension, us for hypoxia, us for sepsis, etc.). certain problem-based us exams can involve scanning of multiple organs to enhance the management of certain patient's problem. the us within this concept is not considered just as diagnostic tool but rather as an integral part of pediatric cardiac intensive care (pcicu) management that involves diagnosis, tailored treatment, monitoring effects, goal-directed therapy, ruling out possible complications, and to guide most of pcicu procedures. this article describes some of the applications of this innovative program over a 6-year period in a pcicu and its impact on patient care.
classification_path: Medical and Health Science > Clinical Medicine > Internal Medicine > Gastroenterology

title: approach to the postnatal sonographic evaluation of prenatally detected abdominopelvic cysts
display_name: Approach to the postnatal sonographic evaluation of prenatally detected abdominopelvic cysts
abstract: prenatally detected abdominal and pelvic masses are commonly cystic in morphology and usually seen on mid-trimester sonography. sonography is the favored imaging modality for the postnatal evaluation of these lesions in newborns, given its availability, low cost, lack of ionizing radiation, lack of sedation, and high spatial resolution in small patients. the differential diagnosis of abdominopelvic cystic masses in newborns is broad given that they can arise from many organs and may have overlapping features on imaging. this article illustrates an approach to the postnatal sonographic evaluation of prenatally detected cystic abdominal and pelvic masses based on their anatomic location and distinctive sonographic characteristics, which can aid in an accurate diagnosis and guide appropriate management.

title: results and complications of surgery for gastro-oesophageal reflux.
display_name: Results and complications of surgery for gastro-oesophageal reflux.
abstract: one hundred and six children undergoing antireflux surgery were studied; 41 were severely mentally retarded and 29 had reflux strictures. although the eventual rate of success was 92%, 20 patients developed complications that required a second operation. prolapse of the fundoplication into the mediastinum was the commonest complication (in seven patients), followed by intestinal obstruction (in five), and intractable fibrous oesophageal strictures (in five). the incidence of postoperative complications was highest in patients with mental retardation or oesophageal strictures. referral of these patients for operation was invariably delayed, and earlier referral may have avoided many of the complications.
classification_path: Medical and Health Science > Clinical Medicine > Internal Medicine > Gastroenterology

title: splenic torsion in heterotaxy syndrome with left isomerism: a case report and literature review
display_name: Splenic Torsion in Heterotaxy Syndrome with Left Isomerism: A Case Report and Literature Review
abstract: splenic torsion is an unusual condition that results in congenital abnormality, especially in the visceral abnormal arrangement. we report the case of an 8.5-year-old boy with features in the right upper quadrant. radiological investigations revealed heterotaxy syndrome with polysplenia and a hypodense tumor in the right upper quadrant adjacent to several spleens. we initially treated it as an intra-abdominal tumor. laparoscopy was performed to check the tumor condition and revealed a congestive tumor located in the abdomen of the right upper quadrant below the central liver, which was suspected to be a torsion spleen without attaching ligaments. laparoscopic splenectomy was successfully carried out without complications. the pathological report shows splenic tissue with hemorrhagic infarction. physicians should be vigilant of the differential diagnosis of the acute abdomen in adolescents.
classification_path: Medical and Health Science > Clinical Medicine > Internal Medicine > Gastroenterology

title: hypertriglyceridemia and megacystis microcolon intestinal hypoperistalsis syndrome
display_name: Hypertriglyceridemia and Megacystis‐Microcolon‐Intestinal Hypoperistalsis Syndrome
abstract: megacystis-microcolon-intestinal hypoperistalsis syndrome (mmihs) is a rare congenital disease characterized by abdominal distention caused by an enlarged and nonobstructed urinary bladder with associated hydronephrosis, microcolon, hypoperistalsis, and malrotation of the small intestine. the condition generally leads to fatality during infancy (1). the cause and pathogenesis of this disorder are not fully understood, and mmihs is not a form of intestinal pseudo-obstruction (2,3). however, vacuolation and smooth muscle atrophy of the intestinal wall have been described (4). no information is available, as far as we are aware, describing intestinal nutrient absorption in mmihs, although these infants require lifelong parenteral nutrition (pn) because of the underlying intestinal dysmotility. we report on an infant girl with mmihs with profound hypertriglyceridemia. a novel technique using differential density gradient ultracentrifugation (ddguc) was used to determine a possible cause of the hypertriglyceridemia. case report a 2540-g infant girl was born vaginally at 33 weeks to a 33-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 2, whose prenatal ultrasound demonstrated a female fetus with massive expansion of the bladder consistent with mmihs. there was no family history of congenital anomalies or miscarriage. percutaneous decompression of the bladder was performed before delivery, and apgar scores were 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes of age, respectively. the infant was noted to have a markedly distended abdomen with no appreciable bowel sounds at delivery. she was unable to tolerate any amount of nasogastric or nasojejunal feeding because intestinal motility was absent, and pn was started as her sole source of nutrition. an upper gastrointestinal barium series demonstrated a lack of peristalsis of the stomach and small intestine and also a malrotation (fig. 1a). a barium enema revealed microcolon (fig. 1b). hydronephrosis, hydroureters, and cortical thinning of both kidneys were noted on renal ultrasound. the patient had an initial elevation of serum creatinine at 1.6 mg/dl, but creatinine levels normalized with scheduled bladder catheterization. at 4 months of age, she underwent a ladd procedure for malrotation, gastrostomy tube placement, diverting ascending loop colostomy, and liver biopsy. the patient did not have biliary atresia or other ductal abnormalities at the time of surgery. the liver biopsy at that time revealed bile duct proliferation, significant cholestasis, and periportal fibrosis but no cirrhosis (fig. 1c).fig. 1: a, upper gastrointestinal barium series revealing minimal peristalsis of barium and presence of malrotation. b, barium enema revealing microcolon. c, liver biopsy specimen revealing portal fibrosis, cholestasis (arrow), and bile duct proliferation (hematoxylin and eosin staining, original magnification 40).the patient's hepatic function deteriorated as she became older. she had an aspartate aminotransferase level of 702 international units per liter (iu/l) and an alanine aminotransferase of 467 iu/l by 6 weeks of age. she became progressively cholestatic with a direct bilirubin that increased to 11.4 mg/dl and a -glutamyltransferase that increased to 153 iu/l by 6 months of age. her triglyceride levels also gradually increased with age. at 3 days of age her triglyceride levels were 70 mg/dl, but by 6 months of age they had increased to a range of 738 to 1560 mg/dl. after removal of lipids from the pn formulation, her serum triglycerides were maintained between 700 and 800 mg/dl. the patient's total cholesterol ranged from 216 to 224 mg/dl, which was slightly above the 95th percentile for her age and sex; however, this value was primarily attributed to very low density lipoprotein (vldl) cholesterol. high-density lipoprotein (hdl) cholesterol ranged from 68 to 77 mg/dl, which was at the 75th to 90th percentile for her age and sex (5). the patient's serum was not noted to be grossly lipemic but had an opalescent yellow color. the maternal triglyceride levels were normal. no information was available regarding the biological father, although there was no history of early atherosclerotic disease in either side of the patient's family. the patient underwent a multivisceral transplant (liver, small bowel, large bowel, and pancreas) at an outside institution at 11 months of age because of intestinal failure, multiple bacterial infections, and eventual progression to cirrhosis with loss of hepatic synthetic function. after transplantation, the patient's hypertriglyceridemia resolved. methods to determine the cause of this patient's hypertriglyceridemia, we used a novel approach to lipoprotein density profiling, ddguc. this approach has been used to study lipoprotein-a particles and involves digital subtraction of 1 lipoprotein profile from another, after selective precipitation of lipoprotein components (6). in this case, an immunoseparation assay kit for remnant lipoproteins (rlp) (polymedco, inc, cortlandt manor, ny) was used, which consisted of an immunoseparation gel containing antibodies to apolipoprotein (apo) b-100 (apob-100) and apoa-1 on sepharose beads in buffer (5 mmol/l tris-hcl). lipoproteins were separated in a self-forming density gradient by use of csbi ethylenediammine tetraacetic acid (csbiedta) and a fluorescence tag solution of n-(7-nitrobenz-2-oxa-1,3-diazol-7-yl)-6-ceramide (molecular probes, eugene, or). the fluorescent tag incorporated into the lipoprotein particles was used to image the position of the different particle distributions as described previously (6 8). in brief, 60 l of the patient's serum was mixed with the rlp immunoseparation gel and 2 l of a 2 mg/ml n-(7-nitrobenz-2-oxa-1,3-diazol-7-yl)-6-ceramide solution in dmso to a total volume of 900 l. inasmuch as the patient could not tolerate any type of enteral feeding, nonfasting pn serum was obtained during pn infusion, and fasting serum was obtained after pn had been stopped for 6 hours. the resulting solutions were incubated in 1.5-ml eppendorf tubes at room temperature for 2 hours in an m-60 orbital mixer (labnet international, inc, edison, nj) at 1400 rpm. after incubation, the rlp fraction was recovered from the supernatant and concentrated by ultrafiltration (8). both the fasting and nonfasting pn serum samples from the patient before and after immunoprecipitation were subjected to ddguc by use of a 0.240 mol/l csbiedta solution to generate the density gradient (6 8). all of the samples were ultracentrifuged at 120,000 rpm for 6 hours at 5 c in polycarbonate tubes in an optima tlx ultracentrifuge tla 120.2 fixed-angle rotor (beckman-coulter, palo alto, ca). after ultracentrifugation, 200 l of water was layered on top of the tube contents for each sample to resolve the lowest density fractions from the meniscus (8). images of the tubes were obtained for analysis and were converted to density profiles (fig. 2a, b).fig. 2: a, density profiles of nonfasting pn serum and rlp fractions in 0.2 mol/l csbiedta. b, density profiles of fasting serum and rlp fractions in 0.2 mol/l csbiedta.lipoprotein fractions were collected after centrifugation by slow immersion of the ultracentrifuge tube in liquid nitrogen. slices were obtained at predefined tube positions by use of a digital micrometer. fractions were thawed and filtered to remove any particulates. the fractions were analyzed by sodium dodecylsulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (sds-page) to determine apob-100 and apob-48 (8). a standard gel electrophoresis protocol was followed for preparation of a 3% to 8% tris-acetate gel (invitrogen, carlsbad, ca). after electrophoresis was completed, the gel was removed, and a standard silver staining method was performed (9). the gel was then analyzed by kodak 1d image analysis software (fig. 3).fig. 3: sds-page analysis with the following lanes: apob-100 standard (a), nonfasting buoyant trl (b), nonfasting dense trl (c), nonfasting pn buoyant rlp (d), nonfasting dense pn rlp (e), fasting buoyant trl (f), fasting dense trl (g), fasting buoyant rlp (h), and fasting dense rlp in a 3% to 8% tris-acetate gel (i). apob-100 is noted in all lanes except the lane containing buoyant nonfasting pn rlp (lane d). note that a small band for apob-48 may be present in lanes f through h but is otherwise not detectable.results the nonfasting pn and fasting density profiles are shown in figure 2a and b. these figures demonstrate both the total lipoprotein profile, which includes the entire population of lipoproteins present in the serum, and the rlp density profile, which represents those lipoproteins whose immunoreactivity to apob-100 and apoa-1 is different from the majority of the lipoproteins (as described in methods). the process of layering with water separates buoyant triglyceride-rich lipoprotein fractions (trl) from dense trl. the features of the lipoprotein density profile included trl such as buoyant vldl, dense vldl, and remnant vldl. other noted features included low-density lipoprotein (ldl), hdl, and serum proteins. overall, the lipoprotein fractions were decreased in the fasting serum; however, the relative intensities of the various lipoprotein fractions remained nearly constant. particles containing apob-48, including chylomicrons or their remnants, were not detectable in the density profiles or by gel electrophoresis, with the exception of minimal intensity noted in the lanes containing buoyant trl, dense trl, and buoyant rlp. the lanes with minimal apob-48 detection possibly could have been attributed to absorption of biliary lipids and lipids from desquamated intestinal epithelium, given that there was no other source of chylomicron synthesis in the patient (10). the main apolipoprotein constituent detected in both the fasting and nonfasting pn buoyant and dense vldl fractions was apob-100 (fig. 3). if chylomicrons and their remnants were present, then the meniscus fraction produced by rlp immunoseparation should have contained chylomicrons and buoyant vldl. we cannot exclude the possibility that these fractions contained exceedingly small amounts of apob-48, inasmuch as the silver staining method can detect even nanograms of apolipoprotein. however, given that normally fed patients demonstrate the presence of apob-48, our patient with mmihs seemed to demonstrate a lack of chylomicron synthesis (8). discussion primary causes of neonatal and infant hypertriglyceridemia are rare. the secondary causes of hypertriglyceridemia include diabetes, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, renal failure, glycogen storage disease, lipid storage disease, and autoimmune disorders (11). hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis also is associated with hypertriglyceridemia in children but was ruled out in this child (12). the most common, albeit rare, cause of primary hypertriglyceridemia is low, or absence of, lipoprotein lipase (lpl) activity caused by a defect in the lipase enzyme or apoc-ii, which is required for lipoprotein lipase activation. these 2 proteins are required for triglyceride hydrolysis contained in chylomicron and vldl particles. genetic mutations of either protein result in severe hypertriglyceridemia, chylomicronemia, and elevated vldl. diagnosis typically is made by measurement of lpl activity in postheparin plasma (eg, after intravenous administration of 60 u heparin per kilogram of body weight) (13,14). chylomicron particles are synthesized in the small intestine, and vldl particles are assembled in the liver and released into the bloodstream. the first stage of catabolism involves activation of lpl on the endothelium of capillaries in adipose and muscle tissue. apoc-ii acts on the surface of the vldl particles, which results in the hydrolysis of associated triglycerides to free fatty acids and formation of rlps (11,15). therefore, the rlp density profiles presented here (fig. 2a, b) provide indirect confirmation of lpl activity and apoc-ii. other techniques, including capillary isotachophoresis, have shown that chylomicrons and vldl particles demonstrate lipoprotein lipase activity (16). the use of ddguc to determine an rlp density profile is simpler than heparin injection for determining the possibility of familial lpl deficiency because it does not require systemic heparinization. previous work has demonstrated that healthy volunteers fed a normal diet produce a ddguc profile that includes trl, intermediate-density lipoprotein, hdl, and serum protein (predominately albumin). such lipoprotein classes separate according to density along the gradient formed from the csbiedta gradient solution. after layering with water, buoyant trl are separated from dense trl. if the same healthy volunteers are fasting, then ddguc shows a separation of the buoyant and dense trl but at a decreased intensity. sds-page analysis of healthy individuals also demonstrates obvious apob-48 and apob-100, even in the fasting state (fig. 4) (8).fig. 4: density profile and sds-page analysis in a healthy control individual. a, density profile in 0.2 mol/l csbiedta of a fasting normolipidemic individual before layering with water. b, after layering with water in the fasting individual. c, rlp density profile in the fasting individual. d, sds-page analysis (in a 3% to 8% tris-acetate gel) of 2 fasting healthy individuals with the following lanes: phosphorylase-b molecular weight standard (a), apob-100 standard (b), buoyant trl from individual 1 (c), dense trl from individual 1 (d), ldl from individual 1 (e), buoyant trl from individual 2 (f), dense trl from individual 2 (g). the buoyant and dense trl fractions and ldl demonstrate apob-100 content. the ldl fraction does not exhibit any apob-48 content, but the buoyant and dense trl fractions do exhibit apob-48 content.the hepatic sinusoidal epithelium should act as a biofilter for lipoproteins; however, this biofilter may be disrupted by changes in the extracellular matrix in the space of disse, such as the hepatic fibrosis as seen in this patient. such changes in the extracellular matrix can affect cholesterol metabolism (17,18). for example, patients with cirrhosis who are fed a carbohydrate-rich meal can produce functioning vldl particles containing the majority of triglycerides if they have preserved hepatic function, although the vldl response becomes impaired as hepatic synthetic function worsens (19,20). cholestatic liver disease also has been associated with hypertriglyceridemia, although excess triglycerides are usually found in lipoprotein (lp)-x and lp-y particles rather than vldl particles (21). advancement of enteral nutrition can prevent the effects of cholestasis caused by pn, but the inherent hepatotoxicity from long-term pn and the inability to promote enteral nutrition because of the patient's mmihs contributed to cholestasis and hepatic dysfunction (22,23). the addition of carnitine to the pn regimen in an effort to increase fatty acid oxidation also did not result in any significant triglyceride reduction, which suggests disruption of the liver sinusoids (24,25). patients with severe intestinal malabsorption and hypertriglyceridemia have been shown to have low plasma cholesterol with high triglyceride levels (unlike the patient described herein), regardless of pn status, possibly caused by disruption of bile acid absorption (26). therefore, although the cause of the patient's hypertriglyceridemia is unclear, the pathogenesis of her lipid abnormalities may have been due to the combined effect of cirrhosis, cholestasis, and disrupted bile acid metabolism because she was unable to tolerate enteral nutrition. the elevated vldl level seen in this patient, despite removal of lipids from the pn formulation, also may have resulted from her underlying hepatic disease, an incomplete fasting state that was not physiologically possible in an infant of this age, or it could indicate a lipid metabolism defect present in this patient with mmihs. additionally, the density profiles using ddguc in this patient demonstrate that vldl synthesis by the liver was intact, and the presence of apob-100 using sds-page confirmed this finding. vldl carries endogenous lipids generated by the liver, and the hypertriglyceridemia seen in our patient may have been caused by excessive vldl synthesis, as can be seen in patients receiving pn regimens with glucose (27). we did note that all of the trl fractions were decreased in the patient's fasting state, which suggests that the liver was efficient in clearing vldl particles. the inability of this child to tolerate any enteral feeding because of her mmihs also may have predisposed her to an absence of chylomicrons and their remnants. apob-48 is the main lipoprotein produced by the human intestine, and it generally disappears after an overnight fast (28). previous animal studies have suggested that chylomicron levels remain unchanged, even during periods of starvation (29,30). the long-term effect of pn on chylomicron formation in a child with an underlying intestinal motility disorder is unknown, and prolonged pn in the absence of enteral feedings could affect chylomicron levels. our findings suggest that the intestinal disease associated with mmihs may have an associated lipid processing defect at the intestinal and hepatic levels in addition to the underlying motility abnormalities (fig. 5) (1,3). however, these data are from only 1 patient with mmihs, and other children with this rare disease should be tested to determine whether a lipid processing defect is present in other children.fig. 5: a, normal pathway of lipid absorption demonstrates chylomicron synthesis and hydrolysis by lipoprotein lipase at the capillary level in which chylomicron remnants are cleared through the liver. chylomicrons and their remnants contain detectable apob-48, which indicates intestinal lipoprotein production. chylomicron remnants are processed in the space of disse. subsequent particles, such as vldl, are synthesized by the liver and undergo hydrolysis by lipoprotein lipase to produce the vldl remnant. both vldl and vldl remnants contain detectable apob-100. b, proposed pathway in the patient with mmihs: there is no detectable apob-48, which suggests a lack of chylomicrons and their remnants. however, vldl and vldl remnants are measurable because of detection of apob-100. chylomicron synthesis and hepatic clearance of their remnants subsequently are impaired. possible aggravating factors include disrupted bile acid absorption caused by cholestasis and an inability to tolerate enteral feeds.in conclusion, this patient with mmihs had elevated serum cholesterol and triglyceride, which is different from other patients with malabsorption who demonstrate low cholesterol with hypertriglyceridemia (26). we further demonstrated that hepatic production of vldl and its catabolism was intact and perhaps overexpressed. rlp density profiling by ddguc indirectly proved that our patient did not have lipoprotein lipase or apoc-ii deficiency. however, particles containing apob-48 (eg, chylomicrons and their remnants) were not detectable in the density profiles or by gel electrophoresis. we are unaware of any reported cases of hypertriglyceridemia in infants with mmihs, and our results suggest that such patients may have a unique lipid processing abnormality associated with the eventual development of liver disease. given that previous studies using ddguc in healthy fasting individuals have demonstrated the presence of apob-48, the inability of patients with mmihs to tolerate enteral feeding may indicate a possible lipid processing defect at the intestinal level and also intestinal smooth muscle atrophy. the method of ddguc provides a safe and useful technique to discover the causes of lipid processing abnormalities in rare disorders such as mmihs.

title: a rare case of anterograde gastroduodenal intussusception caused by migrated percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy feeding tube
display_name: A Rare Case of Anterograde Gastroduodenal Intussusception Caused by Migrated Percutaneous Endoscopic Gastrostomy Feeding Tube
abstract: gastroduodenal intussusception is a critical condition in which stomach protrudes into the duodenum. it is a very rare condition in adults. most common causes include intra luminal lesions in the stomach including benign or malignant tumors of the stomach. most common tumors included are gastrointestinal stromal tumors (gists), gastric carcinoma, gastric lipoma, gastric leiomyoma, and gastric schwannoma. it is extremely rare to be caused by migration of percutaneous feeding tube. a 50-year-old woman with a past medical history (pmh) of dysphagia status post percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (peg) tube, history of spastic quadriplegia, presented with acute nausea, vomiting and abdominal distention, and was found to have gastroduodenal intussusception in computed tomography (ct) scan. condition resolved after retracting peg tube. endoscopy did not reveal any intra luminal lesions. external fixation using avanos saf-t-pexy t-fasteners was performed to prevent recurrence of this condition. most common of causes of gastroduodenal intussusception are gist tumors of stomach. ct abdomen is the most accurate test and upper endoscopy is needed to rule out any intra luminal causes. treatment of choice is either endoscopic or surgical resection. external fixation is essential to prevent recurrence.

title: vi. posters
display_name: VI. POSTERS
abstract: introduction: bronchial asthma is the most common chronic pulmonary disease in childhood.benign hypermobile syndrome (bhms) is also a frequent pediatric pathology that is associated with various symptoms of different systems and organs.the group is heterogenic with worse variants like marfan and ehlers-danlos syndrome, and also benign hypermobile syndrome.the combination of the two diseases in childhood is still not well investigated as well as their impact on each other.the role of tenascin x is investigated as a marker of the extracellular matrix, which is decreased among patients with bhms.both diseases: bronchial asthma and bhms are heterogenetic diseases with polygenic inheritance.this study investigated the role of tenascin x in asthmatics with or without bhms and its impact on respiratory pathology in childhood.material and methods: in our study, 70 patients have been included: 50 patients with asthma and hypermobile syndrome, 10 healthy controls, 10 controls with bhms.all patients were assessed with a clinical investigation, functional tests (pft, echocg), and laboratory tests: cbc, nasal and blood eosinophils, total ige, and tenascin x. conclusion: interesting conclusions and results are provided for the pulmonary pathology, laboratory results, and functional changes among asthmatics and bhms children.

title: evaluation of the predictability of clinical and radiological findings in the diagnosis of malrotation
display_name: Evaluation of the predictability of clinical and radiological findings in the diagnosis of malrotation
abstract: background. to evaluate the predictability of clinical and radiological findings in the diagnosis of malrotation. methods. between 2010 and 2020, children with presumptive diagnosis of malrotation were included. the demographic features, clinical and radiological findings, operative findings and outcome were recorded. the upper gastrointestinal series (ugis) were evaluated by two radiologists. all parameters were correlated with surgical findings to evaluate the predictability. results. seventy patients were included. the presenting symptom was bilious vomiting in 29 cases (41.4%), and atypical symptoms (non-bilious vomiting, food refusal, etc.) in 40 cases (57%). one of the cases (1.6%) was asymptomatic and diagnosed incidentally during ugis. 52 cases had abdominal x-ray and 14 (26.9%) of them were normal. doppler ultrasonography (us) (n=20) revealed evidence of malrotation in 13 cases (65%). the location of duodenojejunal junction (djj) in ugis was compatible with malrotation in 33 cases. 48 (61%) cases underwent surgical exploration; 35 cases had malrotation and seven cases had midgut volvulus. median followup time was one year (0.5-7 years). volvulus has recurred in one case and another case operated for volvulus died because of short bowel syndrome. the statistical analysis for predictability revealed that bilious vomiting (sensitivity: 57.1%, specificity: 82.1%), doppler us (sensitivity: 92.3%, specificity: 75%) and right-sided djj in ugis (sensitivity: 96.8%, specificity: 75%) have highest predictability. conclusions. the bilious vomiting, doppler us findings and right-sided djj have the highest predictability to confirm the diagnosis. however, presenting with atypical symptoms and having atypical or normal findings in ugis do not rule out malrotation.

abstract: congenital hypothyroidism (ch) presenting as acute pseudo-obstruction is uncommon. we report two premature infants presenting with acute bowel obstruction subsequently diagnosed to have ch. both responded well to medical management with thyroid supplementation.

title: enhanced recovery after surgery in congenital duodenal obstruction
display_name: Enhanced recovery after surgery in congenital duodenal obstruction
abstract: abstract background the present study aims to explore the clinical application of enhanced recovery after surgery (eras) in pediatric patients with congenital upper gastrointestinal obstruction (cugio). methods a total of 82 pediatric patients with cugio admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit in kunming children s hospital between june 2017 and june 2021 were enrolled in the present study and divided into two groups: the eras group (n = 46) and the control group (n = 36). the eras management mode was adopted in the eras group, and the conventional perioperative management mode was adopted in the control group. results in the eras group and the control group, the time to the first postoperative bowel movement was 49.2 16.6 h and 58.4 18.8 h, respectively, and the time to the first postoperative feeding was 79 7.1 h and 125.2 8.3 h, respectively. the differences in the above two indicators between the two groups were statistically significant (p < 0.05). in the eras group, the days of parenteral nutrition and the length of hospital stay were 14.5 2.3 d and 18.8 6.4 d, respectively. in the control group, 17.6 2.2 d and 23.1 8.1 d, respectively. the differences in these two indicators between the two groups were statistically significant (p < 0.05). conclusion the eras management model had a positive effect on early postoperative recovery in pediatric patients with cugio.

title: fetal mr in the evaluation of pulmonary and digestive system pathology
display_name: Fetal MR in the evaluation of pulmonary and digestive system pathology
abstract: abstract background prenatal awareness of an anomaly ensures better management of the pregnant patient, enables medical teams and parents to prepare for the delivery, and is very useful for making decisions about postnatal treatment. congenital malformations of the thorax, abdomen, and gastrointestinal tract are common. as various organs can be affected, accurate location and morphological characterization are important for accurate diagnosis. methods magnetic resonance imaging (mri) enables excellent discrimination among tissues, making it a useful adjunct to ultrasonography (us) in the study of fetal morphology and pathology. results mri is most useful when us has detected or suspected anomalies, and more anomalies are detected when mri and us findings are assessed together. conclusion we describe the normal appearance of fetal thoracic, abdominal, and gastrointestinal structures on mri, and we discuss the most common anomalies involving these structures and the role of mri in their study. teaching points to learn about the normal anatomy of the fetal chest, abdomen, and gi tract on mri . to recognize the mr appearance of congenital anomalies of the lungs and the digestive system . to understand the value of mri when compared to us in assessing fetal anomalies .
classification_path: Medical and Health Science > Clinical Medicine > Internal Medicine > Gastroenterology

title: the added value of mdct enterography using oral lactulose solution in detection, characterization, and guiding management of small bowel disorders
display_name: The added value of MDCT enterography using oral lactulose solution in detection, characterization, and guiding management of small bowel disorders
abstract: abstract background small bowel variable symptoms present a diagnostic challenge for both gastroenterologists and radiologists due to si length, overlapping serpentine course and continuous motility. ct enterography was introduced in the last two decades as the cornerstone imaging modality in diagnosing small bowel disorders using a mixture of an oral solution containing water and a gastrointestinal diluting agent. this study aims to demonstrate the added value of mdcte in evaluating and guiding the management of small bowel disorders in order to reduce si-related morbidity and mortality. results data analysis of 80 patient records involved in this study demonstrated the high accuracy of mdcte in detecting different small bowel disorders and their related pathologies, confirmed by laboratory and histopathological analyses. conclusions mdct enterography with oral lactulose solution is now the mainstay of imaging in the detection, characterization, and guiding management of small bowel disorders with great value of low-dose techniques in cd patient s follow-up in order to reduce ionizing radiation exposure.
classification_path: Medical and Health Science > Clinical Medicine > Internal Medicine > Gastroenterology

title: diagnosis and treatment of gastro-oesophageal reflux.
display_name: Diagnosis and treatment of gastro-oesophageal reflux.
abstract: gastro-oesophageal reflux (gor) is defined as the involuntary passage of gastric contents into the oesophagus, and is a common cause of morbidity in childhood.gor is an occasional physiological event in normal adults and children,1 2 but becomes pathological when its intensity or frequency increases or when com- plications arise (for example, oesophagitis, fail- ure to thrive).gor may be primary (due to anatomical or physiological abnormalities) or secondary to other diseases such as urinary tract infection, metabolic disorders, food allergy, etc (see table 1).the increasing avail- ability of lower oesophageal ph monitoring, paediatric endoscopic skills, and newer more effective pharmacological agents has led to a greater awareness of the range of symptoms attributable to gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (gord), and the need for a structured approach to diagnosis and management.presenting symptoms although vomiting is the most common symp- tom of primary gord, it is now recognised that children and infants may present with a wide variety of other symptoms (see table 2).these may be related to oesophagitis, for example, haematemesis, anaemia, chest pain, or general irritability or from respiratory com- plications such as recurrent aspiration pneumonia, apnoea, or stridor.gor may also be a factor in the aetiology of apparent life threaten- ing events.certain seizure-like events or dystonic posturing (sandifer-sutcliffe syndrome) may result from gord.3 clinical assessment the history must establish the nature and fre- table 1 causes of secondary reflux * infective gastroenteritis, urinary tract infection * intestinal obstruction

abstract: introduction: adult midgut malrotation is very rare. the presentation in adults is mostly subtle; the diagnosis is often made on imaging. case report: a 32-year-old man presented with a 3-day history of an irreducible painful mass protruding per rectum, followed by abdominal pain and constipation. the patient was febrile and toxic, with marked signs of peritonitis and complete fullthickness irreducible rectal prolapse. abdominal radiographs showed multiple air-fluid levels. a diagnosis of irreducible rectal prolapse with intestinal obstruction was made. laparotomy revealed complete small bowel gangrene, abnormal rotation of the small bowel 180 around the mesenteric root, hypermobile duodenojejunal flexure and ileocaecal junction and an abnormally mobile caecum lying in the central abdomen. abnormal mobility of the sigmoid colon with a large mesocolon, and a large irreducible rectosigmoid intussusception, was also noted. our patient is probably the first case in literature, which may prompt awareness of simultaneously-occurring disorders of fixation, and preventive steps.

title: what have we learned from patients who have arboleda-tham syndrome due to a de novo kat6a pathogenic variant with impaired histone acetyltransferase function? a precise clinical description may be critical for genetic testing approach and final diagnosis
display_name: What Have We Learned from Patients Who Have Arboleda-Tham Syndrome Due to a De Novo KAT6A Pathogenic Variant with Impaired Histone Acetyltransferase Function? A Precise Clinical Description May Be Critical for Genetic Testing Approach and Final Diagnosis
abstract: pathogenic variants in genes are involved in histone acetylation and deacetylation resulting in congenital anomalies, with most patients displaying a neurodevelopmental disorder and dysmorphism. arboleda-tham syndrome caused by pathogenic variants in kat6a (lysine acetyltransferase 6a; omim 601408) has been recently described as a new neurodevelopmental disorder. herein, we describe a patient characterized by complex phenotype subsequently diagnosed using the clinical exome sequencing (ces) with arboleda-tham syndrome (arths; omim 616268). the analysis revealed the presence of de novo pathogenic variant in kat6a gene, a nucleotide c.3385c>t substitution that introduces a premature termination codon (p.arg1129*). the need for straight multidisciplinary collaboration and accurate clinical description findings (bowel obstruction/megacolon/intestinal malrotation) was emphasized, together with the utility of ces in establishing an etiological basis in clinical and genetical heterogeneous conditions. therefore, considering the phenotypic characteristics, the condition s rarity and the reviewed literature, we propose additional diagnostic criteria that could help in the development of future clinical diagnostic guidelines. this was possible thanks to objective examinations performed during the long follow-up period, which permitted scrupulous registration of phenotypic changes over time to further assess this rare disorder. finally, given that different genetic syndromes are associated with distinct genomic dna methylation patterns used for diagnostic testing and/or as biomarker of disease, a specific episignature for arths has been identified.
classification_path: Medical and Health Science > Clinical Medicine > Internal Medicine > Gastroenterology

title: megacystis-microcolon-intestinal hypoperistalsis syndrome associated with cystic fibrosis and meconium peritonitis in a female neonate 4 days of age case report and review of the literature
display_name: Megacystis-microcolon-intestinal hypoperistalsis syndrome associated with cystic fibrosis and meconium peritonitis in a female neonate 4 days of age – case report and review of the literature
abstract: we present a case of megacystis-microcolon-intestinal hypoperistalsis syndrome (mmihs) in a four days old female infant who presented with abdominal distension, bilious vomiting, massive hematuria and feeding intolerance which was first interpreted as prune belly syndrome (pbs), referred to our department after iatrogenic gastric and colonic perforation. berdon syndrome or mmihs is a rare congenital anomaly characterized by a massive enlarged bladder, distended abdomen, microcolon, functional obstruction of the gastrointestinal tract, and malrotation.

title: cecal volvulus with intestinal malrotation: a rare cause of bowel obstruction
display_name: Cecal volvulus with intestinal malrotation: a rare cause of bowel obstruction
abstract: introduction:cecal volvulus is a rare cause of acute abdomen in adults. it accounts for less than 1% of intestinal obstructions and 25-30% of cases of colonic volvulus. congenital intestinal malrotation is a complex disorder due to incomplete or faulty rotation and fixation of the gut during the fetal life.cecal volvulus associated with intestinal malrotation is a very rare presentation. over 16 cases were reported in the literature. case report:a 44-year-old man with no medical history, presented to the emergency department with a 2-day history of abdominal pain and bloating. on clinical examination, the abdomen was distended and tympanic to percussion, with diffuse abdominal tenderness. abdominal x-ray (standing) showed a distended large intestine with an airfluid colonic level. ct scan showed a markedly dilated cecum measuring up to 14 cm, which were located in the left hypochondrium. a whirl sign and a superior mesenteric pedicle swirl were also noted. emergency surgery was performed. intraoperative exploration revealed a cecal volvulus with a largely distended hypermobile cecum located in the left hypochondrium, with preischemic signs within its wall. all the small gut was right-sided and the large gut left-sided, suggestive of mesenterium commune and intestinal malrotation. a right hemicolectomy withileo-transverse anastomosis was done. the postoperative course was uneventful. the patient is on regular follow up and is doing well. conclusion:we describe a rare case of surgical management of cecal volvulus associated with intestinal malrotation in a middle-aged patient with no medical history. this case highlights the importance of early diagnosis by physical examination and radiological findings to prevent serious complications. emergent surgery was the key to this successful management and surgical resection could offer better results with lesser recurrence rate. bangladesh journal of medical science vol. 22 no. 02 april 23 page : 445-448
classification_path: Medical and Health Science > Clinical Medicine > Internal Medicine > Gastroenterology

title: the coexistence of gonadal dysgenesis with mayer-rokitansky-k ster-hauser syndrome, and dandy-walker variant
display_name: The Coexistence of Gonadal Dysgenesis With Mayer-rokitansky-küster-hauser Syndrome, and Dandy-Walker Variant

authorships.name: Atena Tamimi
institutions: Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences

abstract: background: gonadal dysgenesis, the most common cause of primary amenorrhea, is characterized by absent or underdeveloped ovaries. although the coexistence of gonadal dysgenesis and mayer-rokitansky-k ster-hauser (mrkh) has been reported, it is still quite infrequent. to the extent that authors searched, just one study reported the association between rokitansky sequence and dandy-walker malformation. clinical presentation and intervention: we aimed to report a case with gonadal dysgenesis, mrkh, and the dandy-walker variant. in this care report, the authors reported a 15-year-old girl with primary amenorrhea and underdeveloped secondary sexual properties. her karyotype was 46, xx. the abdominopelvic mri without contrast demonstrated bilateral ovarian agenesis and no uterus or cervix. vagina was normal in length. brain mri was consistent with the dandy-walker variant. conclusion: although some affected chromosomal regions have been identified, further genetic analyses should be performed to elucidate the probable association between these anomalies.

title: caecal perforation with faecal peritonitis - unusual presentation of bochdalek hernia in an adult: a case report and review of literature
display_name: Caecal perforation with faecal peritonitis - unusual presentation of Bochdalek hernia in an adult: a case report and review of literature
abstract: the improper fusion of the postero-lateral foramen of the diaphragm was first described by bochdalek in 1848. the incidence of congenital diaphragmatic hernia varies from1:2000 to 1:5000 live births and bochdalek hernias (bh) account for 75 to 85% of these. although it is a well-known entity in neonates, it is occasionally discovered incidentally in adult patients. until now, a total of around 100 cases of occult asymptomatic bochdalek hernia have been reported. the symptomatic cases are encountered more rarely. colon necrosis among the symptomatic cases was reported in some reports. we discuss the present case since we believe it to be, to the best of our knowledge, the first case of a bochdalek hernia in an adult presenting with caecal perforation and faecal peritonitis and review the published literature about this rare condition.

abstract: a rare entity of non-hiatal type transdiaphragmatic hernias, which must be clearly differentiated from paraoesophageal hernias, are the phrenic defects that bear the generic name of congenital hernias bochdalek hernia and larey-morgagni hernia, respectively. the etiological substrate is relatively simple: the presence of preformed anatomical openings, which either do or do not enable transit from the thoracic region to the abdominal region or, most often, vice versa, from the abdomen to the thorax, of various visceral elements (spleen, liver, stomach, colon, pancreas, etc.). apart from the congenital origin, a somewhat rarer group is described, representing about 1 7% of the total: an acquired variant of the traumatic type, frequently through a contusive type mechanism, which produces diaphragmatic strains/ruptures. apparently, the symptomatology is heterogeneous, being dependent on the location of the hernia, the dimensions of the defect, which abdominal viscera is involved through the hernial opening, its degree of migration, and whether there are volvulation/ischemia/obstruction phenomena. often, its clinical appearance is modest, mainly incidental discoveries, the majority being digestive manifestations. severe digestive complications such as strangulation, volvus, and perforation are rare and are accompanied by severe shock, suddenly appearing after several non-specific digestive prodromes. diagnosis combines imaging evaluations (plain radiology, contrast, ct) with endoscopic ones. surgical treatment is recommended regardless of the side on which the diaphragmatic defect is located or the secondary symptoms due to potential complications. the approach options are thoracic, abdominal or combined thoracoabdominal approach, and classic or minimally invasive. most often, selection of the type of approach should be made taking into account two elements: the size of the defect, assessed by ct, and the presence of major complications. any hiatal defect that is larger than 5 cm2 (the hiatal hernia surface (hsa)) has a formal recommendation of mesh reinforcement. the recurrence rate is not negligible, and statistical data show that the period of the first postoperative year is prime for recurrence, being directly proportional to the size of the defect. as a result, in patients who were required to use mesh, the recurrence rate is somewhere between 27 and 41% (!), while for cases with primary suture, i.e., with a modest diaphragmatic defect, this is approx. 4%.

title: untying the knot: treating recurrent sigmoid volvulus with intravenous levothyroxine
display_name: Untying the Knot: Treating Recurrent Sigmoid Volvulus With Intravenous Levothyroxine
abstract: effect of thyroid hormone dysfunction on gastrointestinal motility is well established. apparat from common presentation of diarrhea and constipation in hyperthyroidism and hypothyroidism respectively, some rare presentations are serious and can lead to significant morbidity and even mortality. sigmoid volvulus is one of them, presenting as a consequence of severe longstanding hypothyroidism. we present a case of relatively young male presenting with sigmoid volvulus and treated with intravenous levothyroxine that resulted in untwisting of the volvulus without surgical intervention and endoscopic de-torsion. j med cases. 2017;8(3):71-72 doi: https://doi.org/10.14740/jmc2750e

title: amelia, dextrocardia, asplenia, and congenital short bowel in deleted ring chromosome 4.
display_name: Amelia, dextrocardia, asplenia, and congenital short bowel in deleted ring chromosome 4.
abstract: we report a female baby with multiple congenital anomalies including left upper amelia, congenital short bowel with malrotation and pseudo-obstruction, dextrocardia with situs solitus, patent ductus arteriosus, and a tiny atrophic spleen. chromosome study showed de novo 46,xx/46,xx,-4, + r(4)(p16-->q22.3)/47,xx,4, + r(4) (p16-->q22.3), + del(4)(pter-->q22.3:). the clinical findings in the patient were probably caused by the interaction of partial trisomy 4pter-->q22.3 or 4p16-->q22.3 and partial monosomy of 4q22.3-->4qter. this karyotype and phenotype have not previously been reported.

title: colorectal polyps and polyposis syndromes
display_name: Colorectal polyps and polyposis syndromes
abstract: a polyp is defined as any mass protruding into the lumen of a hollow viscus. colorectal polyps may be classified by their macroscopic appearance as sessile (flat, arising directly from the mucosal layer) or pedunculated (extending from the mucosa through a fibrovascular stalk). colorectal polyps may also be histologically classified as neoplastic or as non-neoplastic (hyperplastic, hamartomatous, or inflammatory). the neoplastic polyps are of primary importance because they harbor a malignant potential, which represents a stage in the development of colorectal cancer. for this reason, it is essential to identify these polyps at a sufficiently early stage, when a simple outpatient procedure to remove them can interrupt the development of colorectal cancer and prevent disease and death. when invasive carcinoma arises in a polyp, careful consideration must be given to ensuring the adequacy of treatment. although most neoplastic polyps do not evolve into cancer, it is well accepted that the majority of colorectal carcinomas evolve from adenomatous polyps; the sequence of events leading to this transformation is referred to as the adenoma-to-carcinoma sequence. the presence of a systemic process that promotes the development of multiple gastro-intestinal polyps is termed 'polyposis'. hereditary gastro-intestinal polyposis syndromes account for approximately 1% of all cases of colorectal cancer and are associated with a broad spectrum of extra-colonic tumors. early detection and accurate classification of these syndromes are essential, in order to initiate a surveillance program for the early detection of cancer. several polyposis syndromes have been described, each having its own genetic basis and characteristic polyp distribution, clinical presentation, and malignancy risk. diagnostic modalities and treatment options for neoplastic polyps-as well as the most prevalent polyposis syndromes-are reviewed below.
classification_path: Medical and Health Science > Clinical Medicine > Internal Medicine > Gastroenterology

title: superior mesenteric artery syndrome: an uncommon cause of feeding intolerance in infancy
display_name: Superior Mesenteric Artery Syndrome: An Uncommon Cause of Feeding Intolerance in Infancy
abstract: partial gastrointestinal obstruction in infants may be managed conservatively or medically, with surgery reserved for those patients unresponsive to initial treatments. we recently cared for an infant with partial intestinal obstruction caused by superior mesenteric artery (sma) syndrome. case the patient was a preterm infant boy, born at 23 6/7 weeks, with a birth weight of 635 g and apgar scores of 1 and 5 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. he was a product of assisted reproductive technology and a twin gestation. his mother was 32 years old, gravida 1, para 2, with unremarkable maternal laboratory results. his neonatal course was complicated by respiratory distress syndrome, hyperbilirubinemia, grade i intraventricular hemorrhage, patent ductus arteriosus that required surgical ligation, gastrointestinal reflux and feeding intolerance, apnea and bradycardia, necrotizing enterocolitis, retinopathy of prematurity, nephrocalcinosis, hypertension, and bronchopulmonary dysplasia, which eventually led to pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale. his feeding progressed slowly at first, reaching full-volume tube feeds on day of life (dol) 14. on dol 26, continuous feeds were instituted because of a diagnosis of gastroesophageal reflux unresponsive to conservative management and first-line medical therapy. he was given nothing by mouth on dol 41 because of an episode of necrotizing enterocolitis, which responded to gut rest and medical management. trophic feeds were again started on dol 49. by dol 62 he was back to full-volume tube feeds. over the next several weeks, the patient underwent multiple attempts at weaning his respiratory support along with several courses of systemic corticosteroids. he received his first course of systemic steroid treatment (dexamethasone for 5 days) during his third month of life, with a second course (dexamethasone for 5 days) started 5 days after discontinuation of the first course. he received more systemic steroids (prednisolone) nearly every day during his fifth month of life. during the sixth month of life, he continued to receive systemic steroid treatment (dexamethasone). additionally, he received inhaled steroids (beclomethasone) nearly continuously from the third month of life until long after discharge. on dol 112, while still in the neonatal intensive care unit, he took his first feeding by mouth. his oral feedings initially advanced well. however, as his cardiopulmonary conditions worsened he could no longer tolerate oral feedings and progressively required more tube feeds. he eventually required a tracheostomy because of his dependence on mechanical ventilation. after the tracheostomy, oral feeds were restarted. he tolerated small-volume feeds (<25 ml/feed). however, at larger bolus volumes, he again experienced feeding intolerance, this time manifested as frequent, large-volume, nonbilious emesis. he did not tolerate bolus nasogastric feeds but did tolerate continuous nasogastric feeding. there was no evidence of suck-swallow-breath incoordination. formula changes did not improve the patient's condition. an abdominal radiograph showed a massively dilated stomach bubble when he was just over 6 months old (fig. 1). an upper gastrointestinal contrast study was subsequently performed. the results showed minimal reflux in the lower third of the esophagus and dilation of the proximal duodenum with abrupt termination of the contrast column over the mid-spine (fig. 2a, b). a diagnosis of sma syndrome was made. the recommendations were to feed him upright and tilted slightly forward. metoclopramide was discontinued, and lansoprazole was started. a transition was made to ad lib oral feeds during the day, with continuous nasojejunal feeds at night. formula adjustment was required because of diarrhea, which subsequently improved. a repeat upper gastrointestinal study showed pylorospasm and continued dilation of the duodenum. he continued to receive medical treatments for gastroesophageal reflux disease. at the time of discharge he was taking bolus oral feeds during the day and had continuous feeds by nasojejunal tube at night. during the course of his illness, his growth had been steady and appropriate.fig. 1: plain film showing massively dilated stomach bubble.fig. 2: upper gi contrast study: lateral (a) and ap (b) showing persistently dilated proximal duodenum with abrupt termination of the contrast over the mid-spine (third portion of the duodenum) consistent with classic description of sma syndrome.after discharge, his feeding and cardiorespiratory conditions improved. he eventually underwent a transition to all oral feeds and no longer requires specific positioning during and after feedings. he has not required a follow-up contrast study. he is doing well with feedings. his growth is good (he even outgrew his twin sister), and he no longer has symptoms of his sma syndrome. therefore, further gastrointestinal imaging has not been indicated. he was weaned off the ventilator and underwent tracheostomy takedown. he continues to be followed up in the neonatal intensive care unit graduate clinic, and at 18 months he is doing well. discussion the sma syndrome was first described by von rokitansky in 1861 (1a). other terms that identify this syndrome are arteriomesenteric compression, duodenal compression, chronic duodenal ileus, cast syndrome, and wilkie syndrome (1). the syndrome is usually associated with a rapid and dramatic weight loss. the cause is controversial and may include multiple factors. the leading theory is a reduction in the angle formed by the sma and the abdominal aorta, causing entrapment of the duodenum (fig. 3) (2). the altered angle may be due to abnormally low positioning of the sma or to changes in intraperitoneal fat volume or distribution that would usually keep the space between the sma and the aorta wide enough for the intestine to pass through. other explanations include visceroptosis, angulation of the gut at the ligament of treitz and duodenal malrotation (3), and alteration of intestinal motility (4).fig. 3: diagram showing normal relationship of gi tract to sma artery and lateral view showing closure of the angle of the sma with entrapment of the distal duodenum resulting in partial obstruction.in adults, presentation usually includes postprandial epigastric discomfort, eructation, fullness, and large-volume vomiting. the symptoms are often relieved by vomiting or a prone position. there is usually accompanying dramatic weight loss, as can be seen in patients with malignancies, eating disorders, malabsorption, head injuries, cerebral palsy, or spinal deformities. patients are usually older children and young adults; girls and women are more often affected than boys and men. no racial differences have been identified. the syndrome is frequent in anorexic women, trauma patients in the intensive care unit, drug addicts, and patients who have had spinal surgery (5). untreated patients can experience malnutrition and dehydration. the presentation is complicated in neonates because of the inability of these patients to describe their symptoms. our patient had frequent, large-volume, forceful nonbilious vomiting that occurred relatively soon after feedings. his belching was loud and long by infant standards. he did not have dramatic weight loss (fig. 4). however, it is likely that his intraperitoneal fat distribution had been affected by the prolonged corticosteroid treatments he had received for his severe respiratory disease. we speculate that this may have led to a decrease in peritoneal fat and closure of the angle between the sma and the aorta. this is not difficult to believe, in light of the extensive investigation of the effects of cortisol on body fat redistribution. most studies have suggested an increase in retroperitoneal fat related to high doses of corticosteroids. others, however, have shown that steroids alter the pattern of fat deposition, specifically the visceral fat content and ratio of visceral fat to total body fat (6 9). during the course of his illness, the patient received two 5-day courses of steroids during his third month of life and daily systemic steroids for more than 60 days continuously during his fifth and sixth months of life. additionally, he received inhaled steroids nearly continuously from the third month of life until long after discharge. it is possible that the prolonged doses of steroids resulted in disordered adipose distribution throughout his body. inasmuch as it is known that long-term steroid use increases the retroperitoneal fat and the visceral fat contents, it is likely that these opposing forces combined to close the angle formed by the sma at the aorta, resulting in signs and symptoms of sma syndrome.fig. 4: growth chart of infant from birth to day-of-life 220.given the history of steroids in neonatology, one may wonder why this illness has not been previously described, to our knowledge. first, even at the peak of steroid use in preterm infants, rarely did infants receive more than 42 days of treatment. more commonly, steroid courses were limited to 28 days. our patient received an extremely prolonged course of systemic treatment with additional inhaled steroids. second, it is possible that many episodes of feeding intolerance in growing preterm infants who receive steroids may have actually been due to this sma syndrome. because this disease is rare in children, attending physicians in neonatology may not be familiar with this problem and may not have considered it in the differential diagnosis. the argument may be put forth that the sma syndrome in this patient resulted from compression of the artery by the massively dilated stomach, as a consequence of pylorospasm. however, whereas gastric distension is common in crying infants and can cause displacement of the duodenum, it is not likely to result in obstruction. furthermore, the stomach is usually located relatively far away from the retroperitoneal structures. when gastric distension is present, the stomach expands anteriorly, away from the structures in question. posterior expansion to compress the sma would require that the stomach displace the pancreas and other tissues in the area. finally, nasogastric decompression of the stomach for our patient did not relieve the signs and symptoms of obstruction. in patients with sma syndrome, the duodenum is dilated proximal to the third portion with accompanying to-and-fro peristalsis in the proximal duodenum, which is visible by gastrointestinal contrast studies (3). computed tomography of the abdomen, magnetic resonance imaging, ultrasonography, or endoscopy may also be helpful in making the diagnosis (10,11). there is delayed gastric emptying. our patient had a massively dilated stomach as shown on a plain radiograph of the abdomen and clinical signs consistent with partial obstruction. the upper gastrointestinal contrast study results were diagnostic. initial management consists of treatment of any underlying condition causing weight loss or fat redistribution. conservative management consists of gastric decompression and body positioning during and after feeding. left lateral decubitus, knee-chest, and prone positions are often helpful for relieving symptoms in adults. prokinetic agents may help improve motility through the obstructed section of duodenum. for patients unresponsive to conservative or medical management, surgical options may be available. however, these are controversial. our patient responded to conservative management with limited volume of feeds and leaning forward during feeding. more important, as his respiratory status improved, he no longer required frequent systemic steroids, which allowed his fat distribution to return to normal and reopening of the angle of the sma. conclusions sma syndrome in infants is rare but may present with frequent, large-volume, forceful vomiting unresponsive to treatment for gastroesophageal reflux disease. initial treatment for sma syndrome may be conservative, such as specific positioning during and after feedings, or it may require medication. for patients unresponsive to initial treatments, surgery may be required to release the duodenum. physicians should consider this diagnosis in patients with partial gastrointestinal obstruction, particularly if the patient has a coexisting condition that predisposes him/her to disordered adipose deposition, as may be seen with chronic steroid administration for severe bronchopulmonary dysplasia.

title: when intestinal obstruction is not a surgical condition
display_name: When intestinal obstruction is not a surgical condition
abstract: we report the case of a middle-aged man who had undergone two diagnostic laparoscopies with no significant findings after he was attended at the emergency department with cramping pain, abdominal distention and vomiting, with radiological images simulating a small bowel obstruction. after multiple hospitalisations and an extensive set of tests, including a genetic study, he was diagnosed with chronic pseudo-obstruction, an uncommon, unrecognides syndrome with high morbidity. being aware of this pathology can make it easier to diagnose, and thereby, we can avoid unnecessary surgical interventions, because its management and treatment are mainly based on pharmacological therapy. after a proper diagnosis our patient's progression was satisfactory due to the treatment introduced, with no further hospitalisations.
classification_path: Medical and Health Science > Clinical Medicine > Internal Medicine > Gastroenterology

title: megacystis-microcolon-intestinal hypoperistalsis syndrome: a case report
display_name: Megacystis-Microcolon-Intestinal Hypoperistalsis Syndrome: A Case Report
abstract: megacystis microcolon intestinal hypoperistalsis syndrom (mmihs) is a quite rare congenital and fatal disease which was firstly defined by berdon and his colleagues. it appears through a widely enlarged bladder and microcolon and its cause is unknown (berdon et al., 1976; carmelo et al., 2005; makhija et al., 1999; loening-baucke and kimura 1999; redman et al., 1984; hsu et al., 2003; yigit et al., 1996; srikanth et al., 1993). the disease is found in females three or four times more than in males (srikanth et al., 1993; sen et al., 1993; hirato et al., 2003). most of the cases die within the early months of their lives (yigit et al., 1996; srikanth et al., 1993; sen et al., 1993; hirato et al., 2003). we present the case of a female newborn with antenatal ultrasound revealing intestinal mass and bilateral hydroureteronephrosis. the case was admitted for intestinal obstruction after birth.
classification_path: Medical and Health Science > Clinical Medicine > Internal Medicine > Gastroenterology

title: laparoscopic surgery for appendiceal cancer with intestinal malrotation in an adult: a case report
display_name: Laparoscopic surgery for appendiceal cancer with intestinal malrotation in an adult: A case report
abstract: the laparoscopic approach may be safer and less invasive than laparotomy, and extracorporeal lymph node dissection is safe and reliable for patients with intestinal malrotation.

title: small intestinal mucosal fat in childhood enteropathies.
display_name: Small intestinal mucosal fat in childhood enteropathies.
abstract: a sequential series of 100 small bowel mucosal biopsies from children was studied to assess the frequency and pattern of mucosal fat staining, and to compare patterns of fat distribution with mucosal structure and clinical diagnosis. deep mucosal fat was commonly associated with those clinical groups showing normal mucosal structure. while fine granular surface epithelial fat was common in normal and abnormal biopsies, the presence of large fat globules in the surface epithelium was almost entirely limited to biopsies showing villous shortening. large fat globules in the surface epithelium in coeliac disease and cow's milk sensitive enteropathy were probably related to the more severe degrees of villous abnormality encountered in these clinical groups. however, large fat globules in surface epithelium were also found in a few cases of cow's milk sensitive enteropathy with normal or minimal villous blunting. fat staining may be a useful additional histological marker to aid in the interpretation of small intestinal mucosal biopsies.
classification_path: Medical and Health Science > Clinical Medicine > Internal Medicine > Gastroenterology

title: the role of serotonin transporter in human lung development and in neonatal lung disorders
display_name: The Role of Serotonin Transporter in Human Lung Development and in Neonatal Lung Disorders
abstract: introduction. failure of the vascular pulmonary remodeling at birth often manifests as pulmonary hypertension (pht) and is associated with a variety of neonatal lung disorders including a uniformly fatal developmental disorder known as alveolar capillary dysplasia with misalignment of pulmonary veins (acd/mpv). serum serotonin regulation has been linked to pulmonary vascular function and disease, and serotonin transporter (sert) is thought to be one of the key regulators in these processes. we sought to find evidence of a role that sert plays in the neonatal respiratory adaptation process and in the pathomechanism of acd/mpv. methods. we used histology and immunohistochemistry to determine the timetable of sert protein expression in normal human fetal and postnatal lungs and in cases of newborn and childhood pht of varied etiology. in addition, we tested for a sert gene promoter defect in acd/mpv patients. results. we found that sert protein expression begins at 30 weeks of gestation, increases to term, and stays high postnatally. acd/mpv patients had diminished sert expression without sert promoter alteration. conclusion. we concluded that sert/serotonin pathway is crucial in the process of pulmonary vascular remodeling/adaptation at birth and plays a key role in the pathobiology of acd/mpv.

title: torsional necrosis of an output loop internal hernia after roux-en-y choledochojejunostomy: a case report
display_name: Torsional Necrosis of an Output Loop Internal Hernia After Roux-en-Y Choledochojejunostomy: A Case Report

authorships.name: Chao Huang
institutions: Second Affiliated Hospital of Nanchang University

authorships.name: Zhikun Ning
institutions: Second Affiliated Hospital of Nanchang University

authorships.name: Zhengming Zhu
institutions: Second Affiliated Hospital of Nanchang University

abstract: ultra-short bowel syndrome (usbs) refers to a clinical condition characterized mainly by severe diarrhea and nutritional disorders caused by the residual small intestine length of <30 cm (1). after roux-en-y choledochojejunostomy, the output loop herniated from the back of the anti-reverse peristalsis loop, resulting in intestinal torsion and necrosis, and leading to this rare case of internal hernia. patients with torsion often show severe abdominal pain and persistent aggravation, but this symptom lacks specificity, making it easy to be misdiagnosed. acute intestinal torsion and necrosis often lead to large-scale small bowel resection, resulting in usbs. we report a case of torsional necrosis of an output loop internal hernia after roux-en-y choledochojejunostomy, providing certain reference for the diagnosis and management of such cases.

title: meconium ileus in the absence of cystic fibrosis.
display_name: Meconium ileus in the absence of cystic fibrosis.
abstract: although meconium ileus in the absence of cystic fibrosis is considered a rare event, it was found that eight of 37 (21.6%) newborn infants with meconium ileus had no laboratory or clinical evidence of cystic fibrosis.
